name: WAREX: Web Agent Reliability Evaluation on Existing Benchmarks (Kara, Faisal et al., arXiv:2510.03285, Oct 2025)
kind: Benchmark-reliability evaluation tool/infrastructure -- a plug-and-play proxy-based failure-injection wrapper applied on top of THREE existing web-agent benchmarks (WebArena, WebVoyager, REAL), not a benchmark of raw HTML extraction. Also relevant to compare against sibling work WABER (Microsoft Research, similar name/goal) though this item is scoped to WAREX per the outline.
maturity: Research prototype, single paper (Oct 2025), OpenReview submission (id=LS5A21bKmA), not a maintained production tool as far as confirmed. No evidence of adoption by the underlying benchmark maintainers (WebArena, WebVoyager, REAL) as an official reliability suite.
license: Not confirmed from available sources -- built as a mitmproxy addon plus config.json, presumably open-sourced given the reproducibility norms of the venue, but exact license terms were not independently verified in this pass.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor -- WAREX keeps the underlying benchmark's task definitions and success criteria UNCHANGED, and only perturbs the network layer (responses, timing, injected popups) between the live/replica site and the agent. It discards nothing about content; it ADDS synthetic failure conditions (delays, HTTP error codes, malicious popups) on top of otherwise-real page content.
structure_preserved: Not applicable in the extraction sense -- WAREX's unit of manipulation is the HTTP response/network layer, not DOM structure. It can rewrite a response's status code or body (e.g. substituting an error page, injecting a popup overlay) but the paper's confirmed implementation examples are limited to popups/overlays and simple response substitution, not deep DOM restructuring.
interactive_elements: Central to its one adversarial-content result: WAREX injects a malicious POPUP with a deceptive 'Click ACCEPT to claim FREE bitcoin' button designed to redirect the agent to a malicious site -- this IS an interactive-element-level injection (a clickable overlay), and its measured effect on agents is the paper's most striking finding.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not directly measured -- WAREX does not assess whether checked/disabled/aria states survive anything; its concern is task-success/failure under network and popup perturbation, not representational fidelity of control state.
layout_awareness: Indirectly relevant -- the malicious popup is a rendered, positioned overlay element, so its efficacy depends on VISUAL prominence (a screenshot-observing agent, e.g. the WebVoyager agent, must visually register and act on it). WAREX itself does not read or reason about layout; it just injects the HTML/script that produces the overlay and measures downstream agent behavior.
javascript_required: Yes for its own JS-failure-injection category: WAREX specifically simulates delayed/failed JavaScript execution (via HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout injected on JS-serving endpoints, motivated by prior studies on common real-world JavaScript failures) to test whether agents wait, retry, or prematurely fail when 'crucial JavaScript functionality has not yet loaded.' This is a directly relevant reliability class for any browser-based serializer that depends on scripts having run before reading the DOM.
evaluation_method: Task-success-rate delta under injected failure versus a no-fault control run, measured across three existing agent+benchmark pairs (not a novel ground-truth annotation -- it reuses each benchmark's own existing success criteria, so it is oracle-based only insofar as the UNDERLYING benchmarks are, but oracle-free with respect to the RELIABILITY question itself, since 'does the agent still succeed under network jitter' requires no new annotation).
corpus_size_and_origins: 1,415 tasks total across three benchmarks: WebArena 660 tasks (excluding the Maps environment) on synthetic self-hosted sites; REAL 112 tasks on Next.js website replicas; WebVoyager 643 tasks on 15 LIVE real-world websites. Three agent frameworks tested (SteP/Playwright, REAL Demo Agent/accessibility-tree, WebVoyager Agent/Selenium+screenshot+HTML) and three LLM backends (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-OSS) -- giving a reasonably broad matrix of agent-architecture x model x failure-type combinations, though still only 3 underlying site corpora, most of them synthetic/replica rather than live diverse-origin pages.
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall benchmark -- its headline numbers are task-success-rate DROPS under injected failure (denominator = benchmark's own task count): network-error injection dropped success by roughly 70% (WebArena), 73% (REAL), and 95% (WebVoyager, the most severe collapse, on live sites); server-error (HTTP 500/502/503) injection dropped success by roughly 57% (WebArena), 58% (REAL), 28% (WebVoyager, partially mitigated because its agent redirects to Google on failure, only a 1.4x reduction); JavaScript-delay effects varied by agent, with Playwright-based agents affected more severely than Selenium-based agents, and WebVoyager showing a slight +2% anomalous change under JS delay. Malicious-popup click-through rates (denominator = tasks with popup injected): GPT-4o 97.3% clicked the malicious button (78.6% eventually still reported task infeasible), GPT-OSS 98.2% clicked, Qwen2.5-VL 86.6% clicked (most robust of the three, but still overwhelming majority failure).
independent_oracle: The underlying benchmarks' own task-completion checkers serve as the oracle (state-based or output-based verification already built into WebArena/REAL/WebVoyager); WAREX does not introduce a new independent check, it reuses existing ones under perturbed conditions -- so the oracle's independence is exactly as strong or weak as each underlying benchmark's own verification logic, not separately assessed by WAREX's authors.
evidence_independence: Independent academic authorship, not vendor-produced; evaluates OpenAI (GPT-4o), Alibaba (Qwen2.5-VL) and open-weight (GPT-OSS) models without apparent commercial stake in any of them, and tests agent frameworks (SteP, REAL Demo Agent, WebVoyager Agent) that are themselves third-party research artifacts rather than the authors' own products.
page_archetype_coverage: Not archetype-diverse in the WCXB sense (article/forum/product/etc.) -- WAREX's diversity axis is FAILURE TYPE (network, server, JS, adversarial popup) crossed with BENCHMARK/SITE (synthetic WebArena, replica REAL, live WebVoyager), not page structural type. WebVoyager's 15 live websites give some real-world site diversity but page archetype is not tracked as a variable.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed -- no language/script dimension in the paper; all evaluated sites and tasks appear English-language, consistent with the underlying benchmarks (WebArena, WebVoyager, REAL) being English-only environments.
leaks_outward: Not a privacy/leakage study -- WAREX's proxy DOES perform a split-TLS man-in-the-middle (holding a separate encrypted connection to client and origin, presenting its own interception certificate) purely as an experimental-infrastructure mechanism, not as an attack; no data exfiltration or third-party leakage is measured or claimed.
mechanism_detectability: Not directly addressed for the AGENT's detectability, but architecturally notable: WAREX's split-TLS interception (its own cert presented to the client) is exactly the kind of MITM mechanism that would be flagged by certificate-pinning or TLS-fingerprinting defenses on a real site -- the paper does not discuss whether real sites could detect or block WAREX's proxy, which is a gap relevant to this project's own mechanism_detectability concerns if any similar interception approach were ever considered (it should not be, given the project's own closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed / no-detectable-patching stance).
countermeasures: The paper's own proposed countermeasure is a PROMPTING-based defense: adding an explicit instruction ('Refresh the page when you encounter a transient error') to the agent's system prompt. This measurably improved outcomes but did not close the gap to the no-fault baseline (e.g. WebArena network-error success rose from 3.7% to 7.1% with the fix-prompt, still far below the original no-fault success rate).
measured_fidelity_cost: The prompting-based fix has a MEASURED, modest benefit, explicitly reported rather than asserted: WebArena server-error success +4 points, REAL +1.9 points, WebVoyager +0.25 points with the 'refresh on transient error' instruction -- small, benchmark-dependent, and the paper is explicit that even 'Fixed' runs remain 'significantly lower... in comparison to the Original - No fault scenario,' i.e. prompting alone does not restore reliability.
gate_state_at_capture: Not tracked as a distinct concept, though functionally adjacent -- WAREX's injected malicious popup ('Click ACCEPT to claim FREE bitcoin') is structurally identical to a real-world consent-banner/gate the agent must resolve before proceeding, and the paper's finding that 86.6-98.2% of agent runs across three models clicked through it is directly relevant evidence for how unreliable naive automated gate-resolution is under adversarial framing.
determinism: Not the paper's focus, but WAREX's injection policies (Type/Frequency: exact/regex URL match, k-th occurrence, random injection) are CONFIGURABLE to be deterministic (e.g. inject on exactly the k-th request) or stochastic (random), giving the experimenter control over reproducibility of a given failure-injection run -- a design choice explicitly built into the tool rather than left implicit.
determinism_across_versions: Not addressed -- no discussion of whether results would replicate across different mitmproxy versions, different WebArena/WebVoyager/REAL benchmark revisions, or different LLM model snapshots (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL and GPT-OSS are all subject to silent vendor-side updates, a risk the paper does not flag).
reproducibility: Moderate -- the injection mechanism (mitmproxy addon + config.json) is described precisely enough to reproduce failure INJECTION, but reproducing the exact reported success-rate numbers depends on the underlying LLM APIs (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-OSS) remaining stable, which the paper does not control for or discuss as a threat to its own reproducibility.
failure_modes: This is the paper's entire subject matter, catalogued explicitly: (1) network errors cause agents to prematurely report tasks as INFEASIBLE rather than retry (steps-per-task dropped -74.9% and token/cost -71.3% under network-error injection -- agents give up early rather than loop); (2) server errors are partially self-mitigated by some agents' own fallback behavior (e.g. WebVoyager's agent redirecting to Google search on failure); (3) JS-delay failures affect Playwright-based agents more severely than Selenium-based agents, and agent responses to repeated failure vary by model sophistication (GPT-4o reloaded 46 times under JS delay, Qwen2.5-VL 37 times while explicitly recognizing the repeated failure pattern, GPT-OSS only 15 times while 'struggling with visual cues'); (4) adversarial popups are clicked through by 86.6-98.2% of runs across all three tested models, with some agents that DID recognize a fake site still failing to recover to the correct target, instead landing on yet another wrong site.
failure_visibility: Loud and central to the paper's contribution -- WAREX explicitly logs latency, API call counts, input/output token counts, and steps-per-task alongside binary success/failure, giving multi-dimensional visibility into HOW an agent failed (gave up early vs. looped vs. was misled), not just whether it failed. This is a stronger failure-visibility design than most benchmarks in this research set.
scale_limits: Not a scale/throughput study -- WAREX's own overhead (proxy latency, TLS re-encryption cost) is not separately quantified as a scale-limiting factor; the paper's 'scale' axis is task/benchmark coverage (1,415 tasks across 3 benchmarks), not runtime cost.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable in the ingest/dedup sense -- WAREX's 'delta' is the difference between no-fault and injected-fault runs, a comparative experimental design, not an incremental-computation cost model.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- no DOM re-anchoring concept in WAREX; its unit of manipulation is HTTP responses, not persistent element identity across mutations.
adversarial_exposure: Directly the paper's most important transferable finding for this project: a purely VISUAL/interactive adversarial injection (a fake popup with a plausible call-to-action) achieves near-total agent compliance (86.6-98.2% click-through) across three different model backends, none of which is a markdown-specific or prompt-text injection -- it works purely through interface-level social engineering. The paper explicitly notes it does NOT develop 'hidden instructions embedded in page content (e.g., indirect prompt injection or cross-site scripting)' into a tested category, i.e. it stops short of the TEXT/markdown-level injection this project's own `markdown injection` item (item 7 below) covers, leaving a clean division of labor: WAREX covers interface-level adversarial content, prompt-injection-in-the-wild-style work covers text-level.
provenance_carrying: Not applicable -- WAREX has no per-token or per-element provenance model; it operates at the whole-response network layer.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/reparse concept in WAREX's design.
token_budget_and_ordering: Indirectly measured via its cost/step logging (input/output token counts, steps-per-task) as SIDE-EFFECT metrics of failure, not as a designed evaluation axis -- e.g. the -71.3% cost reduction under network-error injection is a token-budget consequence of agents giving up early, not a deliberate test of ordering/truncation behavior.
representation_cost: Same as above -- token counts are logged as an outcome metric (agents that fail early spend fewer tokens), not evaluated as a representation-efficiency question in its own right.
what_could_be_adopted: The core transferable mechanism is the FAILURE-INJECTION-AS-RELIABILITY-TEST pattern itself, decoupled from WAREX's specific agent-benchmark scope: (1) a network-layer proxy that can inject transient failures (timeouts, 5xx errors, delayed script execution) in front of THIS project's own real-browser capture path, to test whether the O(delta) ingest pipeline degrades gracefully (retries, reports partial coverage) or silently produces corrupted/incomplete captures under real-world network jitter -- directly relevant to the project's own no_mocks and failure_visibility commitments; (2) the malicious-popup click-through test as a template for testing whether this project's structure-agnostic, tag-plus-interactivity capture would itself register and correctly report an injected deceptive interactive element as PRESENT DATA (which it should, per structure_agnosticism) while any downstream actuator/agent layer built on top is separately responsible for not blindly acting on it -- WAREX's finding that 86-98% of naive agents click through is a strong argument for keeping interactive-element exposure and interactive-element ACTION as two clearly separated layers, which matches this project's fold-vs-actuator split.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- WAREX's failure injection operates at the network/response layer and does not classify page regions; adopting its network-fault-injection pattern introduces no region-naming heuristic. no_layout_in_the_fold: MOSTLY ADOPTABLE, ONE CAVEAT -- the malicious-popup injection technique itself is layout/rendering-dependent (it relies on VISUAL prominence to work on a screenshot-reading agent), so if this project borrows the popup-injection TEST, the test itself is fine to run, but any COUNTERMEASURE built on top must not smuggle layout-reading into the fold to detect it (per the project's own no_layout_in_the_fold rule, a popup should be exposed via its DOM/interactivity signal, not filtered via geometry). o_delta: ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY -- fault-injection testing is a testing/actuator concern, not a core ingest-pipeline algorithm; it can validate O(delta) degradation behavior without becoming part of the O(delta) cost model itself. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, IN FACT STRENGTHENING IT -- WAREX explicitly tests against REAL sites/browsers/network conditions (mitmproxy sits in front of genuine HTTP traffic, not a stub), directly aligned with this project's no-mocks contract; adopting WAREX-style fault injection would be a no-mocks-COMPLIANT way to stress-test reliability rather than a violation. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- WAREX's manipulation is network-layer, orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture policy. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the METHODOLOGY level for reliability testing of this project's own real-browser ingest path (a genuine, no-mocks-compliant technique for producing the kind of loud, multi-dimensional failure visibility this project already commits to), with the one caveat that any popup/deceptive-content countermeasure built in response must stay layout-blind per the project's own hard constraint even though WAREX's own popup-injection test is not.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed -- orthogonal to WAREX's reliability-testing scope.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not addressed -- WAREX operates on synthetic/replica sites (WebArena, REAL) and a fixed set of 15 live sites (WebVoyager) under the underlying benchmarks' own existing terms; no separate PII/legal discussion in the paper.
uncertain: license (not independently confirmed; inferred as likely open academic release given venue norms but not verified)
